passage: Tuesday night. Nineteen days since the final interview. Karthik from the hiring team shook my hand and said, 'You'll hear from us by Friday, Vandana, promise.' That Friday came and went. I sent a polite follow-up on Monday, short, thanking them and asking about the timeline. Nothing. Today I caught myself refreshing my inbox during dinner and snapping at my brother when he asked me to pass the dal. That's not me. So tonight I did two things. I sent one last note to Karthik: still interested, happy to hear either way. Then I filled in three new applications before I could talk myself out of it. The silence feels like a verdict on me, but it's really just a door someone forgot to close properly. Tomorrow, no refreshing.

qa.q: How many new applications did Vandana fill in tonight?
qa.a: Vandana filled in three new applications.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling while refreshing the inbox during dinner?
qa.a: Vandana felt anxious and hurt by the silence, irritable enough to snap over the dal, which Vandana saw as 'not me'.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Sending one last polite note and then applying elsewhere worked, because it closed the loop without more waiting and put energy into new chances.

qa.q: How might Karthik see the silence from the hiring side?
qa.a: Karthik may be busy or waiting on a decision and may not realise how heavily a missed Friday reply weighs on a candidate who was promised one.

grounding: Shows a hiring contact going quiet after a promised reply, and the wise mix of polite follow-ups, continued applications and refusing to treat the silence as a judgement of self.

passage: Every evening Ojas cycled past the sweet shop in the Karjat bazaar, because Tanuja sometimes sat on its step with her cousins. Some days she waved him over, laughed at his jokes and asked him to drop her at the bus stand. Other days she looked straight through him. Twice she promised to come to the temple fair with him, and twice she sent a last-minute message: 'Next time, pakka.' At the fair, his friend Bablu watched him check his phone again and said, 'You're living on crumbs, yaar.' The next evening Ojas asked her outright, on the step, whether she wanted to spend time with him properly. Tanuja shrugged and said she liked keeping things open. Ojas nodded, said that wasn't enough for him, and from then on took the long road home past the canal.

qa.q: Where did Tanuja sometimes sit in the evenings?
qa.a: Tanuja sat on the step of the sweet shop in the Karjat bazaar, with her cousins.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when Tanuja said she liked keeping things open?
qa.a: Ojas was disappointed and hurt, but also clearer: he had hoped for more and decided the little he was getting was not enough.

qa.q: Which step helped Ojas stop living on crumbs?
qa.a: Asking Tanuja outright what she wanted, accepting her answer, and changing his route home so he was no longer waiting at the shop.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see the arrangement?
qa.a: Tanuja seems comfortable with it, enjoying his attention and rides without committing, which is why she shrugs and prefers to keep things open.

grounding: Shows occasional warmth and broken promises keeping someone hoping, until he asks clearly and walks away when nothing more is offered.

passage:
March 3: Jagdish told Thomas he felt left out when Thomas skipped his graduation dinner. By the end of the talk Thomas was saying, 'So now I'm a terrible partner?' and Jagdish was the one apologising, unsure how the conversation had turned.
March 17: It happened again over a missed call. That night Jagdish opened a notes page on his phone and wrote down what he had said, word for word, and what came back.
April 2: Reading two weeks of notes, Jagdish saw the same shape each time: his worry became his fault. He showed them to his older sister, Shalini, over tea. She read quietly and said, 'You're not imagining this, and none of it is on you.' Jagdish felt steadier than he had in months, and booked a session with the college counsellor for Friday.

qa.q: What did Jagdish start writing down on March 17?
qa.a: Jagdish wrote down what he had said, word for word, and what came back.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling at the end of the March 3 talk?
qa.a: Jagdish felt confused and guilty, apologising even though he was the one who had raised a hurt.

qa.q: What small step helped Jagdish trust his own memory?
qa.a: Keeping word-for-word notes and showing them to Shalini, someone outside the relationship, made the pattern visible.

qa.q: How might Thomas see these arguments?
qa.a: Thomas seems to hear Jagdish's hurt as an attack and turns it back, so in Thomas's version the problem becomes Jagdish's complaint rather than the skipped dinner.

grounding: Shows a partner twisting words until Jagdish feels at fault, and the steps of noticing the pattern, keeping notes, confiding in family and trusting his own perception.

passage: Jatin, sit. Your Sumit Mama is going to tell you something I never told your mother properly. At twenty-one I was seeing a girl from my typing class, Rekha. If I said I was tired, she said I was bored of her. If I said I wasn't bored, she said I was calling her a liar. I went home feeling guilty for things I hadn't done. One evening my friend Iqbal asked, 'Why do you always say sorry after meeting her?' That question stuck in me. I began writing in a small notebook what I had actually said each day. After a month I read it back and saw the same trick on every page. I trusted that notebook more than the fog in my head, and I ended it. So when your friends say something feels off, listen to them, Jatin.

qa.q: Where did Sumit meet Rekha?
qa.a: Sumit met Rekha in the typing class.

qa.q: How did young Sumit feel after meeting Rekha?
qa.a: Sumit felt guilty and confused, going home sorry for things he had not done.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Sumit see the pattern?
qa.a: Writing down what he had actually said each day and reading a month of it back, which let him trust the record over his confusion.

qa.q: What was it like for Iqbal watching Sumit back then?
qa.a: Iqbal noticed Sumit apologising after every meeting and was concerned enough to ask why, which gave Sumit the first push.

grounding: An uncle recalls a partner who turned his words around, and how noticing the pattern, keeping notes and listening to a friend helped him trust his own perception.

passage: Pooja was sure Ankita had cancelled their Saturday plans; she remembered the voice note, remembered crying in the auto afterwards. But in their Andheri flat on Sunday, Ankita frowned. 'I never said that. You're so oversensitive, you invent things.' Pooja felt the floor tilt. It was the third time that month. Later, alone on the balcony, she opened her phone notes. The voice note had been deleted, but her own line from Saturday was there: 'A cancelled again, said work.' She called her college friend Farah and read it out. 'That's exactly what you told me that day,' Farah said. 'You're not making things up.' Pooja wrote the date on a fresh page, and before sleeping looked up the counselling centre near her office, saving its number for Monday morning.

qa.q: Who did Pooja call and read the note to?
qa.a: Pooja called her college friend Farah and read it out.

qa.q: What does 'Pooja felt the floor tilt' suggest about her inner state?
qa.a: It suggests Pooja felt shaken and confused, beginning to doubt a memory she had been sure of.

qa.q: What small steps helped Pooja hold on to what really happened?
qa.a: Checking her own written note, reading it to Farah, dating a fresh page and saving a counselling centre's number.

qa.q: How might Ankita want Pooja to see these arguments?
qa.a: Ankita wants Pooja to see her own memories as invented and oversensitive, which lets Ankita avoid owning the cancelled plans.

grounding: Shows a partner denying remembered events and calling Pooja oversensitive, and the wise steps of writing things down, checking with a friend and seeking counselling.

passage:
'Indu, did I tell you on Tuesday that Dev missed my birthday lunch?'
'You did. You sent me a photo of the empty chair. Why?'
'Because now he says it never happened. He says he came, and I'm too sensitive and mix things up.'
'Usha, I was on the phone with you while you sat there.'
'I know. But when he says it so calmly, I start thinking maybe I dreamed it.'
'That's what the calm is for. You end up doubting yourself instead of asking why he skipped it.'
'So what do I do?'
'Write things down when they happen, with dates. Keep the photos. And the counsellor at the student centre is free on Thursdays. I'll walk there with you.'
'You'd come?'
'Of course. And Usha, you're not mixing things up.'
Usha let out a long breath and opened a new note.

qa.q: When is the counsellor at the student centre free?
qa.a: The counsellor is free on Thursdays.

qa.q: How does Usha feel when Dev denies the lunch so calmly?
qa.a: Usha feels unsure and self-doubting, starting to wonder whether the whole day was dreamed.

qa.q: What would you advise Usha to do next?
qa.a: Keep writing events down with dates, keep the photos, and go to the student centre counsellor with Indu on Thursday.

qa.q: Why might Dev want the missed lunch to look like Usha's confusion?
qa.a: If the lunch becomes Usha's mix-up, Dev never has to explain skipping it, so the denial protects Dev.

grounding: Shows a partner denying a missed event and calling Usha too sensitive, while a friend confirms the memory and suggests notes and counselling.

passage: Hemant's train to Pune for his internship left at 6 a.m., and his bag was already by the door when Arnab's message came at 11 p.m.: 'If you go, I don't know what I'll do to myself.' It was the third threat in a month; the first two had come when Hemant visited his cousins. Hemant's hands shook. He called Arnab at once and stayed on the line. 'I'm taking this seriously. I'm calling your sister Pallavi now so you're not alone tonight.' Pallavi lived two lanes away and went straight over. With Pallavi beside Arnab on speaker, the three of them called a helpline together. Just past one, Pallavi texted: 'Calmer now. I'm staying. Counsellor tomorrow.' Hemant lay awake, sad and scared, but at dawn he picked up his bag. Caring for Arnab didn't mean handing over his future.

qa.q: What time did Arnab's message arrive?
qa.a: Arnab's message came at 11 p.m.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling while lying awake?
qa.a: Hemant felt sad and scared for Arnab and torn about leaving, yet still decided to take the train.

qa.q: Which steps made Hemant's response safe that same night?
qa.a: Hemant stayed on the line, got Pallavi to go over so Arnab was not alone, and joined a helpline call, so real help was involved before morning.

qa.q: How might Arnab see Hemant's trip to Pune?
qa.a: Arnab may feel real fear of being left and treat the trip as abandonment, using the threat to hold on, which is why the distress needed help rather than obedience.

grounding: Shows a partner threatening self-harm to stop a trip, and the wise response of treating the distress seriously, involving family and a helpline that night, and not being controlled through fear.

passage: 'If you go to Rukmini's sangeet, don't bother calling me after,' Sahil said at the gate of Ritu's building in Lajpat Nagar. 'I'll know you never cared.' Ritu had heard versions of this before: when she joined the dance society, when she stayed late at the library. Each time she gave in, and each time the next demand came faster. That evening she sat on the kitchen floor while her mother chopped onions, and told her everything: the gate, the sangeet, the months before. Her mother put the knife down. 'That's not love talking. That's fear being used on you.' Together they found a counselling line for young adults, and Ritu booked a call for the next afternoon. Then she ironed her yellow kurta for the sangeet and set her phone face down.

qa.q: Where was Sahil standing when he made the threat?
qa.a: Sahil was at the gate of Ritu's building in Lajpat Nagar.

qa.q: What might Ritu be worried about as she sits on the kitchen floor?
qa.a: Ritu is afraid and worn down, worried that going to the sangeet will end things with Sahil and that giving in will only bring more demands.

qa.q: What helped Ritu stop being pushed around by the threat?
qa.a: Telling her mother everything, booking a counselling call, and then choosing to go to the sangeet anyway.

qa.q: How does Sahil want Ritu to see her trip to the sangeet?
qa.a: Sahil frames an ordinary outing as proof that Ritu doesn't care, turning it into a loyalty test that keeps control with him.

grounding: Shows a partner threatening to leave unless Ritu complies, and the wise step of bringing in a trusted adult and a counselling line instead of giving in to fear.

passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Omkar, second-year engineering, came in for the second time. In September he described Madhav as 'perfect': flowers at the hostel gate, forty messages a day, talk of meeting Omkar's parents within two weeks. This week he sat with his jacket zipped to the chin. He said that when he asked Madhav for one evening a week to study alone, the messages stopped. Four days of silence, then a single 'u free?' as if nothing had happened. He kept asking me, 'Did I ruin it by asking?' I asked him to list what Madhav did on ordinary days, not the big days. The list was short, and he noticed that himself. Plan: he'll keep a weekly log of steady behaviour, and we meet again next Thursday.

qa.q: How many days of silence followed Omkar's request?
qa.a: Four days of silence followed.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he asked 'Did I ruin it by asking?'
qa.a: Omkar felt anxious and guilty, blaming himself for Madhav's coldness after a fair request.

qa.q: Which step from the counsellor helped Omkar see the pattern?
qa.a: Listing what Madhav did on ordinary days rather than big days, which showed how little steady care there was.

qa.q: How might Madhav see Omkar's request for a study evening?
qa.a: Madhav seems to take the limit as rejection and withdraws warmth, as if affection is only on offer when there are no limits.

grounding: A counsellor records a partner's intense early attention turning to silence when Omkar sets a limit, and the step of judging by everyday behaviour.

passage: Sunday, late. Aadhya, you nearly said sorry again. Three weeks ago Chaitanya booked a surprise weekend in Lonavala, wrote me a song, called me 'the best thing in my life' in front of everyone at the canteen. Tonight I said I couldn't skip my cousin's engagement for another trip he'd planned. And just like that, nothing. Read, no reply. Saw my story, no reply. It's the same swing as after I said no to moving in with him. Huge warmth, then ice the moment I have a limit. Didi read the chats and said, 'Watch what he does on a boring Tuesday, not on a Lonavala weekend.' Didi's right. Boring Tuesdays with Chaitanya are mostly silence. Tomorrow I'm not chasing, and I'm going to that engagement with a clear head.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya book the surprise weekend?
qa.a: Chaitanya booked a surprise weekend in Lonavala.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when the messages went unanswered?
qa.a: Aadhya felt hurt and confused by the sudden silence, and guilty enough to nearly apologise.

qa.q: What would help Aadhya judge the relationship more clearly?
qa.a: Doing what Didi suggested: watching Chaitanya's behaviour on ordinary days rather than on grand gestures like the Lonavala trip.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see Aadhya's limit about the engagement?
qa.a: Chaitanya seems to take the no as rejection and pulls back warmth, perhaps expecting the silence to bring Aadhya back.

grounding: A diary shows adoration switching to silence each time Aadhya sets a limit, and the insight of judging by steady behaviour rather than grand gestures.

passage:
'You're going to the Sunday match again?' Suraj asked from the sofa.
'It's just the old college gang. Once a week.'
'Those guys don't even like me. And your Amma calls every day. When do we get time?'
'We live together, Suraj. We get every evening.'
'Fine. Go. I'll just sit here.'
Jatin stopped at the door. 'Last month it was my cousin's birthday. Before that, Amma's lunch. I've skipped a lot of things.'
'Because you wanted to be with me.'
'Because you sulked every time.' Jatin picked up his kit. 'I'm going. And I'm going to tell Farid what's been happening. I need at least one person outside this flat to talk to.'
'You'll make me the villain.'
'I'll just say what happened.'
Walking to the ground, Jatin rang Farid first.

qa.q: What event is Jatin going to on Sunday?
qa.a: Jatin is going to the Sunday match with the old college gang.

qa.q: What might Jatin be feeling as he stops at the door?
qa.a: Jatin feels uneasy and sad, realising how many family events have been skipped because of Suraj's sulking.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Going to the match and ringing Farid, because it keeps an outside connection who can help Jatin see the pattern.

qa.q: How does Suraj see Jatin's friends and family?
qa.a: Suraj treats them as rivals for Jatin's time and fears that talking to Farid will make Suraj look like the villain.

grounding: Shows a partner slowly pulling Jatin away from family and friends, and Jatin keeping an outside connection and reaching out to someone he trusts.

passage: My name's Siddharth, and it took me most of second year to see it. Tarun never said, 'Don't meet your friends.' He said things like, 'Imtiaz's jokes are a bit cruel, no?' or 'Your hostel group chat is so childish.' So I muted the chat. I skipped the Holi party because Tarun looked hurt. I stopped calling home on Sundays because we were always 'doing something'. By March I was eating in the mess alone most nights. What woke me up was my roommate Imtiaz leaving a sticky note on my laptop: 'Miss you, yaar. Chai at 9?' I went. I cried a little over the chai, which surprised us both, and I told him everything. I haven't worked it all out yet, but I call home again now, and Imtiaz is the one outside line I don't let go of.

qa.q: What did Imtiaz write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Imtiaz wrote, 'Miss you, yaar. Chai at 9?'

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling over the chai with Imtiaz?
qa.a: Siddharth felt lonely and relieved at once, crying a little after months of drifting away from friends.

qa.q: What would you advise someone noticing the same drift?
qa.a: Reach out to one trusted person, as Siddharth did with Imtiaz, and keep that connection even if a partner frowns on it.

qa.q: How might Tarun see the hostel friends and the group chat?
qa.a: Tarun seems to see them as competition and quietly runs them down, so Siddharth pulls away without ever being told to.

grounding: A first-person account of a partner's small remarks cutting Siddharth off from friends and home, and the recovery of reaching back to one trusted person.

passage: In their small flat in Lyon, Nadia had spent the whole evening sighing loudly while Layla packed for a week-long field trip. 'Go, enjoy,' Nadia said, not looking up. 'I'll be fine alone. Like always.' Layla stopped folding a sweater. 'Do you want me to cancel?' The word yes sat on Nadia's tongue, and she recognised what she was doing: the sulk had been meant to make Layla feel guilty enough to stay. Under it was something plainer. She was scared that a week apart would show Layla she didn't need her. Nadia put her mug down. 'No. I was guilt-tripping you. I'm sorry. Could you call me Wednesday night? That's all I actually want.' Layla smiled. 'Wednesday. I'd like that.' Nadia got up and helped her find the charger.

qa.q: How long was Layla's field trip?
qa.a: It was a week-long field trip.

qa.q: What was Nadia afraid of underneath the sulking?
qa.a: Nadia was scared and insecure, afraid that a week apart would show Layla she was not needed.

qa.q: What small step changed the evening?
qa.a: Naming the guilt-trip and asking directly for a Wednesday call, which gave Layla a clear, fair request instead of pressure.

qa.q: What would change for Layla if Nadia had kept sulking?
qa.a: Layla might have cancelled out of guilt and begun to resent Nadia, feeling controlled rather than loved.

grounding: Shows someone using sulking and guilt to keep a partner home, then seeing the fear underneath and asking directly instead.

passage: At the badminton club after practice, Samir stood in the changing-room doorway. 'If you go for pizza with the team again, maybe I'll just quit doubles,' he told Noor. 'Then you can play with them all you want.' Noor zipped the racquet bag slowly. 'Are you asking me not to go, or threatening me?' The question stung. Samir heard himself: he had done the same thing last week about her phone, and the week before about her study group. Every time he got his way, and every time he felt worse. 'I'm... asking,' he said. 'I get jealous when you laugh with them, and I don't really know why.' 'Then ask me. I might say no.' 'Will you skip it?' 'No. But come with us.' Samir hesitated, then stepped aside and picked up his jacket.

qa.q: Where did this scene take place?
qa.a: At the badminton club after practice.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when Noor asked if it was a threat?
qa.a: Samir felt stung and ashamed, hearing himself repeat an old pattern, and admitted to feeling jealous.

qa.q: What small step helped Samir change course?
qa.a: Turning the threat into a direct question and accepting Noor's no instead of pushing harder.

qa.q: How does Noor see Samir's words in the doorway?
qa.a: Noor sees them as a possible threat and names it calmly, wanting a direct request rather than pressure.

grounding: Shows someone using threats to control a partner, then asking directly and accepting a no once the jealousy behind it is named.

passage: Yosef had checked Mira's location four times before noon, sitting in the campus library in Toronto beside an untouched essay. When she didn't answer a text within ten minutes, he had already typed, 'Who are you with?' His friend Kwame glanced at the screen. 'Again?' 'I just worry,' Yosef said. 'It's because I love her.' Kwame waited. Yosef stared at the message, then deleted it. 'Okay. It's not love. When she's out of reach I feel like she's already gone. My dad left like that, one ordinary afternoon.' 'That's real,' Kwame said. 'But she's the one paying for it.' That evening Yosef told Mira what he had been doing and why, and asked her to turn off location sharing. The next morning he booked an appointment at the student counselling office.

qa.q: How many times had Yosef checked Mira's location before noon?
qa.a: Yosef had checked it four times before noon.

qa.q: What is Yosef afraid of underneath the checking?
qa.a: Yosef feels afraid and insecure, fearing Mira will suddenly leave the way his dad once did.

qa.q: Which steps started to change things?
qa.a: Admitting to Kwame that it wasn't love, telling Mira and asking her to turn off location sharing, and booking counselling.

qa.q: What is it like for Mira when Yosef keeps checking?
qa.a: Mira is watched and questioned over ordinary silences, paying for a fear that has little to do with her, as Kwame points out.

grounding: Shows control driven by fear of abandonment, and the wise path of admitting it, talking to a friend, letting go of checking and seeing a counsellor.

passage: The wellness centre smelled of floor cleaner and the marigolds from the morning puja. Lakshmi sat across from Gurleen, a final-year student who ran the peer listening desk on Wednesdays. 'I made Bhavesh give me his email password,' Lakshmi said. 'And I read his messages when he's asleep. I call it caring.' 'What happens in you when you can't see what he's doing?' Gurleen asked. Lakshmi picked at the chair's torn foam. 'Panic. Like he's slipping away and I'll be the one left behind again.' She said it before she could stop herself. 'That sounds frightening,' Gurleen said. 'And the checking isn't fixing it, is it?' Lakshmi shook her head. Together they filled in a referral to the campus counsellor. On the walk back, Lakshmi texted Bhavesh: 'Please change your password. I'll explain tonight.'

qa.q: When does Gurleen run the peer listening desk?
qa.a: Gurleen runs it on Wednesdays.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi feel when she can't see what Bhavesh is doing?
qa.a: Lakshmi feels panic and a fear of being left behind again, which drives the checking.

qa.q: What made Lakshmi's next steps wise?
qa.a: Naming the fear, getting a referral to the campus counsellor, and asking Bhavesh to change the password so the control is given up.

qa.q: What would change for Bhavesh once the password is changed?
qa.a: Bhavesh would get his privacy back and a chance to hear the honest reason, instead of being watched while asleep.

grounding: Shows someone controlling a partner out of fear of abandonment, then admitting it to a peer listener, seeking counselling and giving up the control.

passage: Abebe had written the list three times on the back of a lecture handout: where to stay, what to take, who to tell. Every version stopped at the same question: what would Selam do when he told her? She had smashed his phone in March and screamed at his sister in front of the neighbours. And his parents, back in Bahir Dar, liked her. In the university café in Addis Ababa, Nour read the list and didn't laugh. 'This isn't weakness. It's you planning to be safe.' Together they rang a support line for people in abusive relationships. The worker helped them pick a day when Nour's brother could be there too, and suggested Abebe tell Selam somewhere public, not in the flat. Walking out, Abebe felt afraid, and lighter than in months.

qa.q: Where did Abebe and Nour talk about the list?
qa.a: In the university café in Addis Ababa.

qa.q: What was Abebe feeling while writing the list?
qa.a: Abebe was afraid of how Selam would react and worried about his parents, who liked her.

qa.q: Which steps made Abebe's plan safer?
qa.a: Calling a support line with Nour, choosing a day when Nour's brother could be there, and telling Selam in a public place.

qa.q: How does Nour see Abebe's list?
qa.a: Nour takes it seriously and sees it not as weakness but as Abebe planning to be safe.

grounding: Shows someone who wants to leave but fears the partner and family reaction, and plans the exit with a friend and a support line, putting safety first.

passage: In the empty training room after the evening session, Pradeep finally told Shankar-sir, the batch mentor, why he had been arriving with red eyes. 'Our families fixed the engagement last year. Since then Sunaina decides who I talk to, checks my phone, and says if I break it off she'll tell everyone I cheated. My mother will believe her.' Shankar-sir closed the laptop. 'Thank you for telling me. Walking away from something like this is hard, and wanting to is not weakness.' He wrote down the employee counselling line and a helpline for relationship abuse, and sat with Pradeep while he called the counselling line from the room. They booked a session for the next morning. 'And your mother,' Shankar-sir said, 'maybe tell her with the counsellor's help, before anyone else tells her a story.' Pradeep nodded, shaky but less alone.
